llm_response.content:
Empirical Research Plan  
“Do buyers correctly capitalize expected fuel costs into vehicle purchase decisions?”

------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
------------------------------------------------------------
Chosen strategy: Two–stage least squares (Instrumental-Variables, IV) combined with an event-study style specification.

Why IV?  
– Our treatment of interest (the gasoline price the buyer expects to face over the life of the car) is plausibly endogenous: macro conditions that push gasoline prices up may simultaneously shift income expectations, credit conditions, or preferences for larger cars.  
– We observe strong, plausibly exogenous shifters of retail gasoline prices that are not directly related to individual auto‐purchase decisions: (i) world crude-oil spot/futures prices and (ii) state-level gasoline tax changes.  
– These instruments vary over time and geography, giving the power to purge contemporaneous gasoline prices of demand-side contamination and deliver causal estimates of how fuel-cost expectations affect vehicle choice.

Event-study layer: In addition to the 2SLS “levels” specification, we will estimate dynamic event-time responses around large, sudden gasoline price shocks (e.g., the 2014 oil-price collapse or major refinery‐disruption hurricanes). This will let us verify parallel‐trend style assumptions and visualize adjustment speeds, but the core estimating equation is the IV.

------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control
------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable (endogenous):  
G_it  = log(real retail gasoline price) in buyer i’s county c during purchase week t.  
Key interacted treatment:  G_it  ×  MPG_j  (where MPG_j is the rated fuel economy of vehicle model j). This interaction captures how the price of gasoline changes the relative total cost of owning a low-MPG versus high-MPG model.

Instruments  
Z1_t   = log(WTI or Brent crude spot price) in week t.  
Z2_st  = change in state s’s per-gallon gasoline tax effective in week t.  
(We can also use distance-to-Gulf-refinery × hurricane week indicators in robustness checks.)

Control (counterfactual): Observations whose gasoline prices are shifted less (e.g., buyers in states with no recent tax change, or in weeks without big oil-price moves). Identification comes from comparing these buyers to otherwise similar buyers who happen to face exogenously different retail prices.

Treatment timing: Continuous; every purchase is “treated” to the extent the contemporaneous instrument-driven component of G_it differs from the mean.

------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Instrument relevance: Crude-oil prices and state gasoline-tax changes have a strong first-stage effect on local retail gasoline prices (F-stat ≫ 10). Highly plausible; there is a mechanical pass-through and abundant prior evidence.

A2. Exclusion restriction: Conditional on fixed effects and controls, crude-oil prices and gas taxes affect the buyer’s vehicle choice only through the retail gasoline price channel. Plausibility:  
• World oil prices are set in global markets, not by U.S. auto buyers.  
• Gas-tax legislation is driven by state budget politics, not by contemporaneous automobile demand composition.  
We will still worry about macro confounders (see Threats).

A3. Stable unit treatment value (SUTVA): One buyer’s treatment does not directly affect another’s choice, conditional on controls. Reasonable given the size of the market.

A4. No complier defiers (monotonicity): A higher instrument value shifts gasoline prices in the same direction for all buyers. Valid because pass-through of oil price/tax to retail price is positive everywhere.

A5. Correct specification of expected fuel cost: Buyers use current gasoline price as a sufficient statistic for future prices (or at least react to it). We test robustness with alternative expectation measures (e.g., 12-month futures).

------------------------------------------------------------
4. Threats to Identification & Mitigation
------------------------------------------------------------
T1. Macroeconomic shocks: Oil-price movements correlate with recessions that also change vehicle demand.  
Mitigation: Add flexible calendar-time fixed effects (year-month FE), state-specific linear trends, local unemployment rate, and credit spread controls.

T2. Policy endogeneity of gas taxes: States might raise gas taxes when state budgets are weak, which could correlate with local economic conditions influencing car demand.  
Mitigation: (i) control for state-year unemployment and income growth, (ii) use lead/lag event-study to test for pre-trend, (iii) drop observations within 3 months before tax announcements as a robustness check.

T3. Geographic supply shocks: Refinery outages raise both gasoline prices and local economic uncertainty (e.g., after hurricanes in Gulf Coast).  
Mitigation: include county-by-month FE when exploiting national crude/oil price variation; when using hurricane shocks as instruments, interact time*distance-to-refinery and test balance on pre-outage characteristics.

------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
------------------------------------------------------------
Assume  car_txn.csv  with one row per transaction and  weekly_gas.csv  with county-week average retail price.

```r
# 0. Packages --------------------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)
library(fixest)        # fast high‐dimensional IV
library(lubridate)

# 1. Load & merge data -----------------------------------------------------
tx <- fread("car_txn.csv")            # transaction‐level
gas <- fread("weekly_gas.csv")        # county‐week gas price
oil <- fread("weekly_oil.csv")        # WTI spot price
tax <- fread("state_gastax.csv")      # state‐week tax rate

# harmonise dates
tx[, week := floor_date(as.Date(purchase_date), unit = "week")]
gas[, week := as.Date(week)]
oil[, week := as.Date(week)]
tax[, week := as.Date(week)]

dt <- merge(tx, gas, by = c("county_fips","week"), all.x = TRUE)
dt <- merge(dt, oil,  by = "week",                all.x = TRUE)
dt <- merge(dt, tax,  by = c("state","week"),     all.x = TRUE)

# 2. Variable construction -------------------------------------------------
dt[, l_gas      := log(real_gas_price)]             # treatment
dt[, l_oil      := log(wti_spot)]                   # instrument 1
dt[, gastax     := state_gastax]                    # instrument 2

dt[, mpg_bucket := fifelse(fuel_economy <= 20, "Low",
                    fifelse(fuel_economy <= 30, "Mid", "High"))]

# interaction variable
dt[, gasXmpg := l_gas * fuel_economy]

# 3. Main 2SLS specification ----------------------------------------------
#  outcome: y = 1 if purchased low-MPG (or continuous log(MPG))
dt[, low_mpg := as.integer(fuel_economy <= 20)]

# First stage & reduced form automatically handled by fixest
iv_formula <- low_mpg ~ l_gas | l_oil + gastax + county_fips + week

# high-dimensional FE: county & week
est_main <- feols(iv_formula, data = dt, cluster = ~state)
summary(est_main)

# 4. Robustness: leads/lags event-study around gas-tax changes ------------
dt[, rel_week := as.integer(week - tax_change_effective_week)]
event <- feols(low_mpg ~ sunab(rel_week, 0) | county_fips + week,
               data = dt[abs(rel_week) <= 52], cluster = ~state)
iplot(event)   # dynamic graph of coefficients

# 5. Robustness 2: Alternative instrument – futures price -----------------
dt[, l_fut12 := log(wti_futures12)]
est_alt <- feols(low_mpg ~ l_gas | l_fut12 + county_fips + week,
                 data = dt, cluster = ~state)
etable(est_main, est_alt)
```

Notes:  
• The `sunab()` syntax produces an event-study (Sun & Abraham, 2020) immune to staggered-timing bias.  
• Clustering at the state level addresses serial correlation from state-level instruments.

------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
------------------------------------------------------------
Theory predicts that higher gasoline prices increase demand for fuel-efficient cars.  
Elasticity benchmark: prior literature suggests roughly a 10 ¢/gal increase (≈ 3 %) raises average new-car MPG by 0.2–0.3 (≈ 1 %). Thus I expect:

β ≈ −0.30 (in a regression of log(MPG) on log(gas price))  
or, equivalently, a one-SD ($0.50/gal) gas increase lowers the probability of purchasing a low-MPG (<20) car by about 5–7 pp off a baseline of ~25 %.

Used-car market should show smaller, but still significant, effects because the existing fleet limits choice.

------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (IV)
------------------------------------------------------------
C1: Instrument strongly predicts treatment (F-stat > 10) …… 1  
C2: Exclusion restriction believable after controls ……………… 0.7  
C3: No differential measurement error ………………………………… 1  
C4: Monotonicity (no defiers) ………………………………………… 1  
C5: Stable sample/no selective attrition …………………………… 0.8  

Overall ≈ 4.5 / 5.  Remaining concern is full validity of exclusion restriction; multiple robustness checks are planned to bolster credibility.
